summary: A 1971 note by R. B. Kalin on implementation of interrupt keys, about letting a user interrupt a remote program.

plainLanguage.summary: How a user could press a key to stop a program running on another computer.

questions: how did early networks handle interrupt keys
what is an interrupt sync character
how does ncp handle process interrupts
subtitle: How to interrupt a remote process in the early network

tldr.problem: The NCP protocol could suspend a remote process but had no way to tell the remote system when to switch the input stream from the user process to a supervisory process, causing synchronization problems.
tldr.mechanism: Use a special interrupt sync character (octal 200) placed in the data stream at the correct point, paired with an INS control message that tells the remote system to stop and scan for the character.
tldr.outcome: This provides a clear marker in the data stream itself, unlike trying to use control characters that some systems needed for other purposes.

today: RFC 103 addresses a specific problem in the NCP protocol of early ARPANET. The broader interrupt handling problem was not fully solved until more comprehensive protocol revisions were made later.

sections.title: The Interrupt Problem
sections.content:
In time-sharing systems, the interrupt key (like Ctrl+C) serves two functions: it suspends the user process and switches the keyboard input stream to a supervisory process. Unaccepted input already typed remains buffered for the suspended process, while new input goes to the supervisory routine.

The NCP protocol implements only half this function. It can suspend a remote process through INS and INR control messages, but offers no mechanism for notifying when the data stream should be switched. Because control messages travel on a separate link from the data, the receiving host cannot rely on arrival times to know which input characters belong to the user process and which to the supervisory routine.
sections.plainLanguage: The computer sending commands is like someone calling instructions to a robot. The interrupt key needs to stop the robot and let someone else give commands. The problem is the signal to stop travels separately from the commands themselves, so the robot gets confused about which commands to stop at.

sections.title: The Solution: Interrupt Sync Character
sections.content:
The RFC proposes using an interrupt sync character (assigned the code octal 200) placed directly in the data stream at the exact point where the interrupt occurs. When an interrupt key is pressed, this special character is inserted into the typing sequence.

To handle cases where buffer space might not be available to transmit a message containing the interrupt character, the existing INR/INS mechanism is kept. When the interrupt sync character enters the text stream, an INS control message is sent. The remote NCP receives the INS, immediately suspends the process, scans the input stream for the sync character, and switches the stream to the supervisory process.
sections.plainLanguage: The solution is to put a special marker character right in the stream of commands at the moment of interrupt. The remote computer sees this marker and knows to stop and switch to a supervisor. If the marker gets stuck in traffic, a separate control message backs it up.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content:
The RFC acknowledges the solution's limitations. It only works with seven-bit ASCII character streams and does not cover EBCDIC or other character sets. It requires the remote system to scan all data on interruptable connections, which must be set up when the connection is created.

The technique is also vulnerable if INS control messages or messages containing the sync character fail to reach the remote host due to network failure, blocked links, or insufficient allocation. In such cases, the remote process might loop indefinitely.
sections.plainLanguage: The solution has some weak spots. It only works with certain character codes, and if the special marker or its backup message gets lost in the network, the remote computer won't know to stop.
